body_html:
Learning how to flirt in Spanish is less about memorizing pick-up lines and more about tone. Spanish can sound beautifully warm and playful, but a phrase that works between friends in Madrid might sound odd in Mexico City, and a line that feels flattering in a song can feel intrusive on the street. Here are natural ways to flirt in Spanish, the slang you will hear, and the habits to avoid.

Key takeaways
  • Specific, sincere compliments work better than dramatic lines.
  • Me gustas is the clear, romantic “I like you”.
  • Flirting slang varies by country: ligar in Spain, coquetear almost everywhere.
  • Unsolicited street compliments (piropos) are often unwelcome. Read the room.
{{toc}}

How to flirt in Spanish: the words you need

The standard verb is coquetear, understood everywhere. In Spain you will hear ligar (to flirt or to pick someone up) and tirar los tejos (to make a move on someone). In Mexico and Colombia, echar los perros means to make your interest obvious. Someone flirty is coqueto or coqueta. The RAE dictionary entry for coquetear is a nice reminder that the word implies playful charm, not pressure.

Compliments that sound natural

SpanishEnglishNotes
Me encanta tu sonrisa.I love your smile.Safe and warm
Tienes una risa contagiosa.You have a contagious laugh.Specific and kind
Qué bien te queda ese color.That colour really suits you.quedar bien = to suit
Eres muy interesante.You’re really interesting.Compliments the person, not the look
Me caes genial.I really like you (as a person).Friendly, a good first step

Playful lines to start a conversation

  • ¿Puedo invitarte a algo? Can I get you a drink?
  • Perdona, ¿te conozco de algún sitio? Sorry, do I know you from somewhere? (A classic, best said with a smile.)
  • Tengo que confesarte algo: no sé bailar salsa. ¿Me enseñas? I have to confess something: I can’t dance salsa. Will you teach me?
  • ¿Vienes mucho por aquí? Do you come here often? (Cheesy in any language, which can be the point.)
{{image:2}}

How to say “I like you” in Spanish

This is where many English speakers stumble. Gustar works backwards: the person you like is the subject. So “I like you” is me gustas, not me gusta tú.

  • Me gustas. I like you (romantically).
  • Me gustas mucho. I really like you.
  • Me encantas. I’m crazy about you / you delight me.
  • ¿Te gusto? Do you like me?

Be careful with me caes bien: it means you like someone as a person, which can sound friendly rather than romantic.

{{book:love-slowly}}

Flirting by text

Much flirting now happens on the phone. A few natural messages:

  • No dejo de pensar en nuestra conversación. I can’t stop thinking about our conversation.
  • ¿Qué haces? Me acordé de ti. What are you up to? You crossed my mind.
  • Tengo ganas de verte. I’m looking forward to seeing you / I want to see you.

You’ll find abbreviations, emojis and tone tips in {{link:texting-in-spanish|texting in Spanish}}, and affectionate nicknames in {{link:spanish-terms-of-endearment|Spanish terms of endearment}}.

Piropos: a word of caution

A piropo is a flirtatious compliment, sometimes poetic, sometimes crude. Traditionally they were shouted at women in the street, and many people today consider that harassment. Some countries have even passed laws against street harassment. A compliment in a conversation you are both enjoying is very different from a comment thrown at a stranger. When in doubt, don’t.

{{image:3}}

Common mistakes when flirting in Spanish

  • Estoy caliente for “I’m hot”. It means aroused. For the weather, say tengo calor.
  • Estoy excitado for “I’m excited”. Also sexual. Use emocionado.
  • Calling someone mami or papi too early. Common between couples in some countries, but forward or vulgar from a stranger.
  • Overusing guapa. In Spain it can even be a casual greeting among friends, so it may not carry the meaning you intend.

A sample conversation

Here is how a light, friendly flirt might sound at a party. Notice how much of it is simply curiosity:

  • A: Perdona, ¿esta canción es de tu playlist? Tienes buen gusto. (Sorry, is this song from your playlist? You have good taste.)
  • B: Jaja, sí, me encanta. ¿Te gusta la música latina? (Haha, yes, I love it. Do you like Latin music?)
  • A: Me encanta, pero bailo fatal. ¿Me enseñas un paso? (I love it, but I dance terribly. Will you teach me a step?)
  • B: Vale, pero luego me invitas a algo. (Okay, but then you buy me a drink.)
  • A: Trato hecho. (Deal.)

Nothing in that exchange is a “line”. It is humour, a small confession and an invitation, which is exactly why it works.

Regional flavour

Flirting vocabulary shifts from country to country. In Spain, someone attractive is guapo or guapa, and estar bueno is a much more physical compliment that you should use carefully. In Mexico, guapo works too, and chulo or chula means cute. In Argentina you will hear lindo and linda constantly, and in Colombia bonito and bonita are warm, everyday compliments. When you travel, listen for the words locals use with each other and borrow them gently.

Body language and timing

Spanish-speaking cultures often feel warmer and more physical than English-speaking ones: people stand closer, touch an arm while laughing and greet with a kiss on the cheek. That warmth is not automatically flirting, so don’t read too much into it. Real interest usually shows in follow-up: someone asks for your number (¿Me pasas tu número?), suggests meeting again or keeps the conversation going long after it could have ended.

Read the moment

Good flirting in any language is a conversation, not a performance. Notice whether the other person is enjoying it, ask questions, and accept a no, gracias gracefully: Sin problema, ¡que lo pases bien! (“No problem, have a good time!”). If things go well, you may soon need {{link:first-date-in-spanish|first date phrases in Spanish}}. For many more real-life situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

Final thoughts

To flirt in Spanish, be specific, be kind and be yourself. A sincere me encanta hablar contigo (“I love talking to you”) beats any line from a song, and it works in every Spanish-speaking country.

faq.q: What is the Spanish word for flirting?
faq.a: Coquetear is the standard word everywhere. In Spain people also say ligar, and in Mexico and Colombia echar los perros means making your interest obvious.

faq.q: How do you say “I like you” romantically in Spanish?
faq.a: Say me gustas. Me caes bien means you like someone as a person, which can sound friendly rather than romantic.
Unsolicited street piropos are widely considered harassment today. A compliment inside a conversation you are both enjoying is a different thing.
